newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany plans new law to ensure cattle slaughter.
newsitem.headline: Germany plans new law to ensure cattle slaughter.

text.p: German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert said on Wednesday he wanted to introduce a permanent order for the slaughter of cows imported from Britain and Switzerland after an emergency decree ran into legal problems.

Borchert told the parliamentary committee for food and health the order would replace the emergency measure, agreed after a new mad cow disease scare, which has been ruled unlawful by several local courts.

New fears about bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, were sparked in Germany last month after officials said they thought they had found the first German-born cow to die of the disease.

The discovery of the cow, thought to have been infected by its British mother, prompted federal and state agriculture ministries to agree to slaughter over 5,000 cattle from Britain and Switzerland -- the countries with the most native BSE cases.
The cow was the fifth to die of the disease in Germany.

But the origin of the cow was later cast into doubt, causing farmers to protest against the mass slaughter and consumer organisations to accuse Bonn of not exerting sufficient control over the import of animals and feed.
Genetic tests on the cow should be completed next month. If it is shown to have been infected by its mother, officials could order the cull of around 12,000 offspring of imported cattle.
Several local courts have ruled that the emergency decree was unnecessary because all cattle from Britain had already been registered and could not be slaughtered for meat or sold.
